name: Sauda
bio: Sauda was born at Delhi about 1720, according to the book, a soldier by profession, much esteemed in his lifetime and a favourite at Court. He is said to have excelled in all kinds of poetry, chiefly the ghazal, the qasidah and satire; the book glosses the name Sauda as the folly of love.

The 3 pieces given here are drawn from Hindustani Lyrics (London: The Sufi Publishing Society, 1919), in the English verse of Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook. They are free renderings, not literal translations, and the original Urdu poems are untitled; each is named here by its first line.

poems.title: Shall I or shall I not console my heart
poems.author: Sauda
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
Shall I or shall I not console my heart
    And win relief?
Or shall I sit in solitude apart
    Nursing my grief?

O hear, while of my life now nearly done
    Some sparks remain!
Soon I may be, who knows, O Cruel One,
    Speechless with pain.

How can I to the fisher speak my thought?
    Her snares are set,
My fish-like heart is by her lashes caught,
    As in a net.

Look on my sorrowful mien, O Love, and tell
    My hopelessness,
None of the manifold troubles that befell
    Can I express.

Fair is the garden, Sauda, to thy view,
    More fair appears
Her dwelling; let me all its ways bedew
    With happy tears.

poems.title: I, like a poor fakir
poems.author: Sauda
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
I, like a poor fakir,
Wander from door to door,
Bearing my load of pain;
But thou, O Ever-Dear,
Thou comest never more
Unto my door again.

poems.title: O changing Wheel of Fate, what thing is there
poems.author: Sauda
poems.translator: trans. Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook (1919)
poems.text:
O changing Wheel of Fate, what thing is there
Thou hast not in thy myriad cycles brought!
Wilt thou, indeed, I wonder in despair,
Bring me at last what I so long have sought?
